title: Asun
author: Anu Odebunmi
desc: Grilled goat chopped into bites, then tossed with peppers and onions fried fifteen minutes until they lose their water — finished when the onions caramelise a bit.
longDesc: Asun is the party dish — chunks of smoky grilled goat in a coarse pepper and onion mixture, eaten with a toothpick and a cold drink. The sequence matters: the meat is cooked and grilled whole first, then chopped, so the smoke gets into it before the surfaces multiply. The peppers and one onion are fried for about fifteen minutes until they have lost their water, the meat goes in for ten, and a second chopped onion goes in at the end for freshness. It is done when those onions have caramelised a little.
ingredients: 1 kg cooked and grilled goat meat
Scotch bonnet (atarodo) peppers — as much as you can tolerate
// Used in the method but not listed in the original
steps: Coarsely blend or chop the peppers and one onion, and set aside.
Chop the grilled goat into bite-sized chunks.
Heat a wok or skillet. Add oil, then the peppers and onions.
Saute with the seasoning and salt about 15 minutes, until the peppers lose their water.
Add the meat and fry 10 minutes.
Add the second chopped onion and stir.
Add more green peppers if using, and fry 5 to 6 minutes until the onions caramelise a bit.
chefTips: Grill the meat whole and chop it afterwards. Chopping first multiplies the surfaces and you lose the smoke into the fire.
Fifteen minutes until the peppers lose their water. If there is liquid in the pan when the meat goes in, the meat will steam instead of frying.
Coarse, not smooth. Asun should have visible pieces of pepper clinging to the meat.
The onions caramelising is the cue. Not browning, not burning — just turning sweet at the edges.
The second onion goes in near the end for bite and freshness. Both onions cooked down and you have lost that contrast.
Female native goat works best, according to another named source — the meat cooks fast and the skin is softer.
Traditionally asun is smoked, not grilled. The smoked version is the real thing and this is the domestic approximation.
commonMistakes: Chopping the goat before grilling it.
Adding the meat to a wet pepper mixture.
Cooking both onions down to nothing.
Overcooking the meat, which is already cooked and grilled.
sources: Adapted from 'Asun Recipe- Spicy Peppered Goat Meat', published on sisijemimah.com. ATTRIBUTION IS DOUBLE AND SHOULD BE RECORDED AS SUCH: the recipe appears on Sisi Jemimah's site but is credited in the text to 'Anu', a friend who the author says makes 'the best Asun' and who shared the recipe with her. Quantities as printed: 1kg Cooked and Grilled Goat meat, Scotch Bonnet (Atarodo) peppers 'as much as you can tolerate', Green and Bell Peppers (Optional), 2 Large Onions, 2 Knorr Chicken Cubes, salt to taste.

Times as printed: saute the peppers and onion about 15 minutes 'until the peppers lose their water'; add the meat and fry 10 minutes; add the second onion and more green peppers and fry 5 to 6 minutes 'until Onions caramelise a bit'.

LIST/METHOD MISMATCH, flagged: vegetable oil appears in the method but not in the ingredient list, so its quantity is unknown and has not been estimated. Second mismatch: the method adds 'more green peppers' at the end, but green peppers are marked optional in the list, so that final addition has no quantity and no guaranteed presence.
YIELD INCONSISTENCY in the original: the recipe states 1 kg but the author notes she scaled it to 4 kg for the photographs, so the stated quantity and the pictured batch do not match.
DECLARED DEVIATION: the recipe uses 'Cooked and Grilled' goat. The traditional smoked variant is mentioned as unavailable to the cook, so this is an acknowledged departure from the canonical dish.

A second named source, 1Q Food Platter's 'Asun – My Owambe Party Favourite', gives NO QUANTITIES WHATSOEVER — goat meat, scotch bonnet, onion, seasoning cubes, salt and 'little water', all unmeasured. Its useful contributions are the sequence (grill the meat whole, chop after) and a cooking tip worth having: 'Female "native" goat works best for Asun. The meat cooks fast and the skin is softer.' Both are reflected in the tips above.
reheating: Hot pan, briefly. It is better slightly charred than gently warmed.
healthBenefits: Goat is leaner than beef or lamb and lower in saturated fat.
High in iron, zinc and B12.
Capsaicin from the scotch bonnets is associated with raised thermogenesis.
culturalNote: Asun belongs to the owambe — the Yoruba party — and it arrives on a tray with toothpicks, to be eaten standing up with a drink in the other hand. The word itself points at smoke, and the smoked version made over a drum is what the dish aspires to; grilling is what most kitchens can manage. It is bar food as much as party food, and it is almost never a main course.
